instructions: Read the passage and choose one answer for each question.
passage:
Iris and Ken are preparing a short article for a fictional community newsletter. It will describe how neighbors repaired a bench near the town garden. Before publishing, Iris reads the headline: “Three Hundred People Built a New Garden.” The number and the description seem different from the notes she took at the event. Ken agrees that every fact in the headline must agree with the text. They decide to verify the numbers before sending the story.

The first paragraph says thirty neighbors helped clean and repair one bench. A later passage says they also planted two small trees. Iris uses a link to open the club's own event record, which lists thirty names and describes the same work. The source is useful because someone recorded it immediately after the event, but Iris still wants to compare it with a second set of notes. She does not assume that one document is always complete or correct.

Ken checks a picture and its caption. The image shows a painted bench, but the caption says that it was a new building. They can zoom in on the picture or enlarge it on the screen; neither action tells them when it was taken. Iris asks the photographer for the original note. With that evidence, they change the caption to “Neighbors beside the repaired bench.” They also correct the claim about three hundred people, since the available record supports thirty.

The draft includes an advertisement for a local paint shop. The publisher has placed a clear label above it so readers can distinguish it from the article. The publication also has a short quote from a gardener: “We enjoyed working together.” A citation identifies the interview where the words came from. Ken wants to forward the draft to the group, but Iris asks him not to send the photograph yet. The people in it have not all given permission for their images to be shared.

They discuss privacy before posting. The club's rule says they must receive permission before publishing an identifiable picture. They should also ask whether anyone wants a name removed. One person may agree to the picture but prefer not to be named; another might ask for the photograph to stay private. Those possibilities are not proof that either person has already made a request. Iris suggests a version without faces while they wait for replies.

The finished newsletter will include a short note about how they checked the story. Readers can choose to subscribe, print a copy, or leave a comment. An icon opens the reading controls, but it does not tell readers whether a claim is true. Ken says that media can offer helpful information and can also show bias when important details are missing. The result of their check is a smaller, more accurate story. The people and newsletter in this exercise are invented.
